title: Chapter 29 – A Foundation of Embers
html:
[Lin Clan – Patriarch Lin Zhenshan]

Eighty-eight parts in a hundred, and the pill has held.

Lin Zhenshan sits on the black cushion in the round chamber with his palm laid flat on the anchor plate and his whole life folded into a space the size of a plum. He has never been so tightly packed. Every year of Qi he has ever gathered, every dawn on the hill, every winter's hard breathing, is being pressed together in his lower field, and it is going well. It is going better than it has ever gone. At sixty-eight his channels tore at seventy percent, and at ninety-four they tore at ninety-one, and both times he lay for weeks and learned patience from the ceiling. This time the walls are bound by a pill that has no flaw in it, and the seed is hard and bright and almost finished.

Eighty-eight. He permits himself a very small, very dry smile. Little builder. What did you do to it?

Then the hill speaks to him.

It is a thing he has never told anyone, not even his wife, who was clever enough to guess it: that for a hundred years he has been able to feel the stone. Not well. Not much. A great slow ache, like a toothache in a mountain, and under it, always, the hum of the vein. In the chamber, with a pill in him and his sense drawn out to its widest, it is as if he had grown roots. He feels the yard through his sit-bones. The wall through his spine. And he feels the pins.

He feels them die.

One by one, in the first hour, he had felt the ring being drawn like a bow: Jian's hand, clever and small and steady, pulling a line here, a line there. He had felt the road fold. He had felt, and nearly laughed aloud at, the pit swallowing the shield block, and a part of him had said: That is my grandson. That is my grandson. Then three pins had gone out together, burnt through like candles, and something very cold had passed through the stone.

Now it passes again. Three more. A blow, a long ragged pressure, a Foundation Establishment palm laid on the air above his head, and the ring is half gone.

Lin Zhenshan opens his eyes.

Six pins. He knows what will follow. He has counted it already, in the dark, three times. Heng will not wait out a full quarter hour. He is not a patient man; he has simply been playing one. When the ring is at its thinnest, he will step in, and he will take the hut, and in the hut is a boy of nine.

The seed is at eighty-eight. He needs another hour. He does not have another hour. He has, perhaps, a quarter of one.

Then I have a choice.

He has known the choice for a long time. He has carried it, wrapped like a coal in wet cloth, since the day his father put a hand on his shoulder in a cold room and told him the last secret of the Patriarch's chair.

It is not in the book. It was never written down.

The Green Pine Breathing Method, as every Lin child knows, has nine breaths. The nine are in the library, on the third shelf, in the founder's own square seal-hand. Lin Shoucheng taught them to his sons. But Shoucheng also taught his eldest a tenth, in the year before he died, with his own lips against the boy's ear, and said: Pass it by mouth, to the one who sits in the chair, and to no one else. And pray that none of you ever has to use it.

The Ember Breath. It is the last breath of a man who has nothing left. It does not gather Qi. It does not store it. It lights it. All the years that a man has not yet lived, all the winters stacked in him like firewood, burn at once, and for as long as the fire lasts, a cultivator who has no right to be Foundation Establishment is Foundation Establishment, with no foundation under him at all.

If the hill must be held, and there is nothing left to hold it with, the old man said, there is always this.

He had, as a boy, assumed his grandfather was being poetic.

Lin Zhenshan weighs the cost. He has done so before. Five years, perhaps six, that is what the healers say he has: five or six winters in a body that is a hundred and ten years old and has begun to hurt in the mornings. It is not a lot to spend. It is only everything.

And the seed. The compressed Qi in his field is not a foundation, but it is a fuse. A thing at eighty-eight parts in a hundred is a thing that will burn very well.

He takes his palm from the plate.

The signal comes up through the stone, as it has every five minutes since dawn: three short, one long. Stay. Faint and clumsy and faithful, as if from the end of a very long cord. His grandson is holding the hill with both hands.

I know, little builder. He rises from the cushion. His joints crack like old kindling. Hold on. I am coming up.

* * *

He breathes.

It is not like the other nine. The other nine are a river, and a man floats on them. This one is a spark, and a man falls into it. He draws in as far as his ribs allow. He holds it. And then, with the whole of his will, he turns the river that has been running into him for eight hours, and for the first time in a hundred years of cultivation, he does not gather. He lets go.

The seed bursts.

The pain is not what he expected. He expected it to be terrible, and it is: a fire that begins at the navel and runs to the tips of the fingers, the soles of the feet, the root of every tooth. But it is also clean. It is very clean. It is the pain of a lamp being lit in a house that has been dark for a century. He feels his channels widen, his bones lighten, his hands stop shaking. He feels the stone of the chamber come alive around him, bright with warmth, and the Qi pours out of him, golden-red, into the air, and the air takes it and shines.

His hair stirs in a wind that is not there.

Foundation Establishment. He tastes the word, a hundred and ten years late. So this is what it is like. Mm. It is a good deal like being young.

The window of it is not long. He can feel the fire eating at the edges of him, a quick bright hunger, a little more with every breath. An hour, perhaps. Perhaps less. A man who burns his years has the strength of a god for the time it takes to boil a pot of tea, and then he is ash.

He climbs.

Forty steps. He counts them, as he has counted them a thousand times. At the fiftieth year of his chair, when his knees began to go, he took them one at a time, with a hand on the wall. Tonight his feet do not touch half of them. At the thirtieth, the warmth is a roar; at the thirty-fifth, the light of his own body throws his shadow up the stair ahead of him like a banner. At the thirty-ninth he slows.

The fortieth step is dark and plain in the glow of his Qi. He stops on it, and kneels, which his knees permit this once, and lays his right hand over the hand of his grandfather.

For a hundred years he has done this, once a year, on the night of the autumn festival. The stone has always been cold. It is cold now.

"Grandfather," he says. His voice has gone strange and young. "I am going to go and hold the hill now."

The stone is silent. But the silver-white lines beneath his palm do not quite look as they did, for just an instant, as if they had pricked up their ears.

He rises, and goes up into the light.

* * *

[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The nosebleed started an hour ago. He has stopped noticing it.

He sits with his back against the wall of the hut and the bronze key crushed in his right fist so hard that the edge has cut his palm. Blood has run down his wrist and into his sleeve. It does not matter. What matters is the number, and the number is wrong.

```
Pins: 6 of 12
Ring integrity: 52%
Load: 88% / 91% / 94% (rising)
Estimated time to failure: 5 min
Subject: Lin Zhenshan — status: UNKNOWN (signal lost)
```

He does not know what happened. For six hours the plate has hummed under his hand like a sleeping animal, and then, three minutes ago, it stopped, and then it screamed. A torrent of heat, a spike and a roar. And now, up the stairs, from a very long way down, something is coming. He can feel it on the key as one feels thunder in the soles of the feet. A column of red-gold fire, climbing.

Grandfather.

The panel flashes:

```
[Scan — Lin Zhenshan (passive, via anchor plate)]
Stage: Compression ABORTED at 88%
State: Foundation Establishment-equivalent (TRANSIENT)
Qi density: 8.9× QR peak (comparable to subject Zhao Heng, 95%)
Fuel source: lifespan reserve (rapid depletion)
Reserve: 5.2 yr → 5.0 → 4.9
Estimated duration: 50 min
CE: +6 (total: 152 / 400)
```

He's burning himself. The last word on the panel makes him go cold. Lifespan. He thinks of the old flask, the pine and plum wine, the hand on his shoulder. He thinks, with perfect clarity, that if he had known, he would have said no. And that this is exactly why no one told him.

The door of the hut stands shut. Behind it, on the other side of the bar, the stairs have begun to glow.

Up they come, step by step, with a sound of boots, steady as a drum. He has heard that step ten thousand times in the corridors of the house, and it has never sounded like this. It sounds like a man who is walking toward a wall he has made up his mind to go through.

The bar lifts from the door by itself. The old oak swings open.

Lin Zhenshan stands in the doorway.

He is not the man who went down. The deep-green robe is the same, and the old plain sword at his hip, and the white head. But the stoop has gone. He is straight as a spear, and taller than Jian remembered, and his skin has the light of a lantern in it. A faint golden haze moves about him like heat above a road, and his eyes are two coals.

"There you are," says Grandfather.

It is his own voice. That is what undoes Jian: it is only his own voice, a little dry, a little amused. "I thought I told you not to look at the door."

"Mother said that."

"Your mother is a woman of great sense." The old man steps in. The floor of the hut shines where his feet fall. He crouches, with an effort that costs him nothing, and lays one hot, dry palm against the side of Jian's face, and wipes at the blood with his thumb. "Your nose. That will be the strain on the key. It will stop when the ring does."

"Grandfather. Your..."

"Don't."

"I can see it."

For a moment the old eyes fill with something so fierce and so tender that Lin Jian can't meet them. "I know you can," says Grandfather. "I told you I would never ask. I will not tell either. It would spoil the afterwards." He touches the boy's forehead with his forehead. "Listen now. You have the key. There are six pins. Heng is at the south edge. He will come in if I am in the way of the door, because he has wanted to see this hut all his life, and because he thinks he knows how a tired man dies."

"He'll kill you."

"He will try." The old man's mouth quirks. "I want you to open the ring for me. At the south, a gap the width of a door. Hold it open. Let me walk out, and let him walk in behind me."

"In?"

"Into the ring. Inside the six."

Lin Jian stares at him. Then, slowly, the shape of it comes up in his head, as a picture comes up in a dish of water.

Six pins, in a hexagon. Heng's shell, twelve paces. The ring, ten. If a man whose Qi is as wide as Heng's stands at the very center of six pins that are all fed from one key, every one of those pins will push inward at once.

A pulse. Not a wall; not a hold. A shout. A hexagon shouting at a man in the middle of it, all six voices in the same breath.

```
[DRY RUN :: Ring collapse (6 pins, all inward)]
Run 1: pulse at palm strike — Foundation jolt 1 heartbeat, success 83%
Run 2: pulse at sword entry — success 41%
Run 3: pulse at 1.5 s after contact — success 12%
Cost per run: Qi 0.40 (no material consumed)
Key integrity after real pulse: DESTROYED (100%)
Ring pins after real pulse: DESTROYED (100%)
```

He's seen it already. The cold thought comes with a certain reluctant pride. He built the plan around a number he can't read.

"The key will not survive," says Lin Jian.

"No."

"The ring neither."

"No. It is a thing made to be used once." Grandfather's eyes are very warm. "I am sorry. I know what the pins cost you."

"I can make more pins."

The old man looks at him for a long moment, and then, to his great surprise, he laughs, a bright, boyish crack of laughter that fills the small hut, and Lin Jian feels the ring shake with it.

"Yes," says Grandfather. "Yes, little builder. I expect you can."

* * *

The ring parts.

It is done in a breath: two pins swinging their light aside in a long soft arc, like a curtain drawn back. A south-facing doorway ten feet wide opens in a wall of blue. Through it the world appears in a rush, noon sun, smoke, blown dust, the gate with its tangle of fallen shields and the figure of Zhao Heng standing at the edge of the ring with his hands behind his back, perfectly composed.

Lin Zhenshan walks out of the hut and into the sun.

A sound goes through the yard. It is not a cheer. It is something lower. A great sigh, from the tower, the wall, the gateway, as if a hundred people had remembered at once that they could breathe. Along the parapet the village guards go to their knees without being told. On the tower Mao has taken his hat off. Old Hu, kneeling in the dust of the gateway with his bent rod across his lap, lifts his face and begins, very quietly, to weep.

Zhao Heng's brows go up.

"Zhenshan," he says. "My goodness. You did it."

"I did something," says Grandfather. "I wouldn't call it that."

"It isn't foundation. I can see that." Heng walks a pace nearer, head tilted, with real interest and without a trace of fear. "It's a lamp, isn't it? You've lit your own lamp. Old fool. How long can you keep it burning?"

"Long enough," says Grandfather. "Come and see."

He draws the sword.

It is not a spirit weapon. It is a straight plain blade of black iron, notched twice near the point and reground so many times that the edge is the width of a coin shorter than when Shoucheng carried it. The Lin sword. The sword that a boy of fifteen takes down from the wall in the hall and swings, and puts back, and that the clan has been carrying for a hundred and fifty years without ever once calling it by name.

Where the light of Grandfather's Qi touches it, it burns red-gold, like iron drawn out of a forge.

"Come in, Heng," he says. "You've waited a lifetime. Come and look at my door."

Zhao Heng smiles.

He is not a fool, and he knows a bait when it is held to his mouth. But he is also nearly two hundred years old, and he has never, in all that time, been beaten by anyone, and the last man on earth who could have done it is standing in front of him with half an hour to live. And behind him is the hut, and what is under the hut, and a hundred and seventy years of wanting. He steps through the gap in the ring.

Come on, thinks Lin Jian. He is on his feet now, with his back to the wall and the key shaking in his bleeding hand, and the six pins glow in his sight like a hexagon of cold stars. A little more. A little more.

Grandfather takes a step back, and a step, as an old man does who cannot quite keep his feet. And Zhao Heng follows, easily, smiling, into the heart of the ring.

Now, he thinks. No. Not yet.

The jade ring flashes on Heng's right hand. He lifts his palm.

And Grandfather's sword goes through his left shoulder like a spit through a fowl.

Nobody sees it start. One moment the old man is stumbling backward; the next he has turned, a single movement, in the open air, and the red-gold blade is through the brown robe and out of the back of the shoulder, and Zhao Heng, who has not been touched in a hundred and twenty years, makes a small surprised sound.

The shell flares. The sword sinks deeper.

Heng's right hand comes round, palm flat, like a door slamming, and the blow catches the old man under the ribs. Lin Jian hears the bones go: three, four, five, a dry crackle like green wood. The old man staggers and does not fall. A bright thread of blood runs from the corner of his mouth, and he is smiling, and he does not let go of the sword.

"The pulse," whispers Lin Jian. "Run one."

He is watching Zhao Heng's shell, not Zhao Heng. A hundred and twenty years of Foundation Qi is a beautiful thing at close range, a vault of smooth gold that has never been cracked. It is also, for an instant after a strike, a thing that has just put the whole of itself into one palm, and for that instant, like a drawn bowstring, it is spent.

Palm strike. Shell recast. Now.

```
Window: 0.31 s
Pulse: ARMED
```

"Now, little builder," says Grandfather.

Lin Jian pulls.

All six pins fire inward in the same instant.

It is not a sound. It is the absence of one: for the length of a heartbeat the whole hill goes quiet, as if every stone had breathed in at once. Then a ring of white light, thin as a hair, shuts from every side on the man at its center, and Zhao Heng's shell rings, like a bell struck by a thousand tiny hammers, and the long beautiful golden vault that has not been broken in a century gives out a tiny crystalline note and goes dim.

The key explodes in Lin Jian's hand.

It does not make a noise. It simply goes black and brittle, like a burned leaf, and a wave of feedback comes up through his arm and through his skull and throws him backward into the wall of the hut. He hits it with his shoulder. He hears something in his right arm give, a wet, hot, shocking snap, and then the arm is not there anymore. He slides down the stones. He tries to lift his head.

He sees it through a red haze.

Zhao Heng is on one knee in the dust with the sword through his shoulder. His shell is gone. He is staring in blank incomprehension at his own hand, and in front of him Grandfather has put one foot forward and is standing very straight in the light of his own flame.

"Mm," says Grandfather conversationally, and drives the blade forward.

It goes in below the navel. A third of the sword goes in, a hand's breadth, and no further, because the old man's arm is shaking and because he has no strength left to push it. But it is enough. Something in Zhao Heng goes out. Not his life. Something larger. The dantian of a late-stage Foundation cultivator is not an organ. It is a place, the room in the body where the Qi lives, and the red-gold iron goes through the door and sets the house on fire.

Zhao Heng screams.

Lin Jian has never heard a sound like it. It is the voice of a man hearing the sound of a bell break that has hung over his house for two hundred years. His whole body arches. A fan of golden light bursts from his mouth and eyes and fingertips and goes out, like water poured onto a hot stone. He falls backward off the blade, in the dust of a yard where nothing has ever fallen, and lies there with his eyes open to the sky.

```
[Scan — Zhao Heng]
Foundation: FRACTURED (dantian breach)
Qi leak: 4.1%/min and rising
Recovery estimate: years (uncertain)
CE: +4 (total: 156 / 400)
```

The yard is silent.

Grandfather stands over him with the sword hanging at his side, bleeding from the mouth, swaying a little. He is breathing in short shallow breaths. The golden haze around him is thinner now, and the light in his eyes has begun to flicker.

Zhao Heng turns his head.

It takes a long time. He looks at the old man. He looks at the broken ring. Then his gaze drifts, slowly, across the yard, to the foot of the stone hut, where a small boy is slumped against the wall with his right arm hanging limp and blood on his chin, and rests there.

It is not the look he gave the slit. It is not mild. It is the look of a man memorizing the face of a stranger in a crowd.

"Zhenshan," he says, in a voice that has gone old. "How long?"

"Long enough," says Grandfather. "Come and see."

Heng closes his eyes.

When he opens them again, he gets up. It is dreadful to watch: a man who has not been hurt in a century, rising from the dust with one hand pressed to his belly and the other hanging, in a brown robe stained black to the waist. He does not take his guards' arms. He walks, alone, down the length of the yard to the gate, past the kneeling Hu and the silent cousins, and nobody moves to stop him. At the bottom of the hill four men of the Zhao household run to meet him, and the chain man, already halfway over the south wall with his coil of chain, turns and flees.

Hoofbeats, going down the road. Then silence.

The cicadas begin again.

It is a single sawing note, in a pine to the east. Then another. And then the whole hill is shrilling with them, a mad, joyous, ridiculous noise, and on the tower Uncle Mao throws back his head and laughs until the tears run down his face.

* * *

Lin Jian watches the world come back in pieces.

Old Hu is staring at his hands. The rod lies on his knees, folded in the middle like a piece of rope, and he is turning it over and over, with a baffled, bereaved tenderness, as if it were a dead child.

Father has gone down to the gatehouse on his knees. He has Feng's head against his chest and is saying something, over and over, very low, and Feng is saying something back, hoarse and impatient and perfectly intelligible. Alive. The word goes through Lin Jian like warm water. He's alive. He's talking.

And from the tower, a small figure in a working short robe is running.

She runs like a girl. He has never seen her run. She comes down the tower stair in three leaps, across the yard, past the fallen shields and the groaning guards, her braid flying loose and one sleeve torn, and she does not look at Grandfather, or at the ruined ring, or at anything else. She goes down on her knees in front of him and takes his face in both her hands.

"I told you," says Su Qinghe, "to come and find me."

"I couldn't walk."

She laughs. It is a short, broken sound, half a sob, and her hands are shaking against his cheeks. "Your arm."

"It's not there."

"It's there. It is only asleep. Third Aunt will..." She stops. She puts her forehead against his. She is shaking all over, and he has never felt anything so wonderful in his life.

Behind her, Grandfather has lowered the sword. It hangs from his hand, the point trailing in the dust. He is looking at the sky, at the white noon over the pine tops, with the expression of a man at the end of a long road.

His hair has turned white. Not gray: white, entirely, snow-white, from the root. The golden haze is almost gone. The firelight in his skin is guttering. He is thinner than he was a quarter hour ago, and there is a transparency about his face, as of paper held to a lamp.

"Well held, little builder," he says.

Lin Jian can't answer.

"Wenyuan." Grandfather does not raise his voice. Across the yard, Father lifts his head. "Take your wife. Take the boy. Take care of what is yours."

"Father..."

"In a moment." A shadow of the old dry humor crosses the lined face. "Jian. Come here."

He cannot stand. Mother gets an arm around him, and the two of them go across the yard, half walking, half sliding, to where the old man stands in the ruin of the ring. The ground is warm under his feet. He puts out his good hand and takes the one that hangs at Grandfather's side. It is hot as a stove, and as dry as paper.

"Now," says Lin Zhenshan. "Help me down the steps. There is something I still have to tell you, and I don't think I have long to tell it."
